'''''Allium ampeloprasum''''' is a member of the [[onion]] genus ''[[Allium]]''. The wild plant is commonly known as '''wild leek''' or '''broadleaf wild leek'''. Its native range includes southern Europe, southwestern Asia and North Africa, but it has been cultivated and [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in many other countries.

''Allium ampeloprasum'' has been differentiated into five cultivated vegetables: [[leek]], [[elephant garlic]], [[pearl onion]], kurrat, and Persian leek.

==Etymology==
The specific epithet ''ampeloprasum'' derives from the Greek ''ampelos'' ("vine") and ''prason'' ("leek"), literally meaning "vine-leek" or "leek of the vineyard".<ref>{{cite web |title=Allium ampeloprasum, Wild Leek |url=https://www.first-nature.com/flowers/allium-ampeloprasum.php |website=First Nature |access-date=19 April 2026}}</ref>

== Description ==
Wild populations produce bulbs up to {{Convert|3|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} across. [[Scape (botany)|Scapes]] are round in cross-section, each up to {{Convert|180|cm|abbr=on}} tall, bearing an [[umbel]] of as many as 500 flowers. Flowers are urn-shaped, up to {{Convert|6|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} across; [[tepals]] white, pink or red; [[anthers]] yellow or purple; [[pollen]] yellow.<ref name="laksdf909wer9">{{Cite eFloras |1 |242101330 |Allium ampeloprasum |family=Liliaceae |first1=Dale W. |last=McNeal Jr. |first2=T. D. |last2=Jacobsen}}</ref><ref>Gleason, H. A. & A.J. Cronquist. 1991. Manual of the Vascular Plants of Northeastern United States and Adjacent Canada (ed. 2) i–910. New York Botanical Garden, Bronx.</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
Allium ampeloprasum is an ecologically diverse species complex and the progenitor of several key cultivated varieties, including the common leek (''A. porrum L. sensu stricto''), characterized by its robust "pseudostem," and the ''A. kurrat Schweinf'', which is grown for its slender leaves. Despite their physical differences, these forms remain closely related to, and fully interfertile with, the wild tetraploid A. ampeloprasum, which is widely distributed in the Mediterranean basin.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zohary |first1=Daniel |last2=Hopf |first2=Maria |last3=Weiss |first3=Ehud |title=Domestication of Plants in the Old World |date=2012 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-954906-1 |page=171}}</ref>

The plant's [[Native species|native]] range is southern Europe to southwestern Asia and North Africa,<ref name="powo"/> including all countries bordering the [[Black Sea|Black]], [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]], and [[Mediterranean Sea]]s from Portugal to Egypt to Romania. In Russia and Ukraine, it is considered invasive except in [[Crimea]], where it is native. It is also native to Ethiopia, Uzbekistan, Iran and Iraq.

It is considered naturalized in the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Czech Republic, the [[Baltic States]], Belarus, the [[Azores]], Madeira, the [[Canary Islands]], Armenia, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, China, Australia (all states except [[Queensland]] and [[Tasmania]]), Mexico, the Dominican Republic, [[Puerto Rico]], Haiti, the United States (southeastern region plus [[California]], [[New York State]], [[Ohio]] and [[Illinois]]), [[Galápagos]], and Argentina.<ref name="powo" /><ref name="laksdf909wer9" /><ref>{{BONAP|genus=Allium|species=ampeloprasum}}</ref><ref>{{Cite eFloras| 2| 200027520 |Allium porrum |volume=24| last1=Xu| first1=Jiemei| first2=Rudolf V. |last2=Kamelin}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Allium ampeloprasum [Aglio porraccio] - Flora Italiana |url=http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=allium+ampeloprasum |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=luirig.altervista.org}}</ref>

The species may have been introduced to Britain by prehistoric people, where its habitat consists of rocky places near the coast in south-west England and Wales.<ref name="pfof">{{PFAF}}</ref><ref>CHRISTOPHER D. PRESTON, DAVID A. PEARMAN, ALLAN R. HALL (2004) Archaeophytes in Britain Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society 145 (3), 257–294 {{doi|10.1111/j.1095-8339.2004.00284.x}}, p. 264</ref>

== Conservation ==
The plant is protected by law in [[Israel]]<ref>{{cite book |author-last=Shmida |author-first=Avi |title=MAPA's Dictionary of Plants and Flowers in Israel |publisher=MAPA |year=2005 |location=Tel-Aviv |pages=237 |language=he |oclc=716569354}}</ref> as well as [[York County, Virginia|York County]], [[Virginia]], where it is commonly known as the "[[Yorktown, Virginia|Yorktown]] onion".<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Yorktown Onion |url=http://www.yorkcounty.gov/CountyGovernment/BoardofSupervisors/BoardsandCommissions/HistoricalCommittee/YCHC/YorktownOnion.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811233135/http://www.yorkcounty.gov/CountyGovernment/BoardofSupervisors/BoardsandCommissions/HistoricalCommittee/YCHC/YorktownOnion.aspx |archive-date=2016-08-11 |access-date= |website=www.yorkcounty.gov}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Allium ampeloprasum'' is the source of several vegetables, most notably:
* [[Leek]] (var. ''porrum'')
* [[Elephant garlic]] or great-headed garlic (var. ''ampeloprasum'')
* [[Pearl onion]] (var. ''sectivum'')
* Kurrat (var. ''kurrat''),<ref name="pfof" /><ref name="prota">Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen.</ref> Egyptian leek or salad leek. This variety has small bulbs, and primarily the leaves are eaten.
* Persian leek (''A. ampeloprasum'' ssp. ''persicum''). A cultivated allium native to the Middle East and Iran, grown for culinary purposes and called ''tareh'' in Persian. The linear green leaves have a mild onion flavor and are eaten raw, either alone, or in food combinations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mousavi|first1=Amir|last2=Kashi|first2=Abedolkarim|last3=Davoodi|first3=Daryoush|last4=Shariatpanahi|first4=Mohammad Sanei|title=Characterization of an Allium Cultivated in Iran: The Persian Leek|date=2006|jstor=20794599|journal=Belgian Journal of Botany|volume=139|issue=1|pages=115–123}}</ref>
Some sources (especially archeological ones) refer to each of these as a separate species,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zohary |first1=Daniel |title=Domestication of plants in the Old World: the origin and spread of domesticated plants in Southwest Asia, Europe, and the Mediterranean Basin |last2=Hopf |first2=Maria |last3=Weiss |first3=Ehud |date=2012 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780199549061 |edition=4th |location=Oxford |page=195 |quote=The more robust varieties grown for their thick ‘pseudostem’ (''A. porrum'' L. sensu stricto) and the slender leafy forms (sometimes referred to as ''A. kurrat'' Schweinf.), are all closely related to, and inter-fertile with, the wild and weedy tetraploid forms of wild ''Allium ampeloprasum'' L., which is widely distributed in the Mediterranean basin.}}</ref> but they are now united as ''A. ampeloprasum''.

== In culture ==
The plant is mentioned as ''shaḥm el-arḍ'' in an 11th-century [[Mishnah]] commentary.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nathan ben Abraham |title=The Six Orders of the Mishnah: with the Commentaries of the Rishonim |volume=1 |page=s.v. ''Sheviit'', ch. 7 |year=1955 |editor-last=Sachs |editor-first=Mordecai Yehudah Leib |contribution=Perush Shishah Sidrei Mishnah – A Commentary on the Six Orders of the Mishnah |place=Jerusalem |publisher=El ha-Meqorot |language=he |oclc=233403923 |author-link=Nathan ben Abraham I}}</ref>
